newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine troops rescue Japanese after shootout.
newsitem.headline: Philippine troops rescue Japanese after shootout.

text.p: Philippine troopers rescued a Japanese businessman on Monday after killing two of his kidnappers in a gunbattle on a southern mountain, officials said.

At least three Filipinos accompanying Kenichi Takayama, 49, were also rescued by soldiers and police after a dramatic chase on Sarangani island, where they were kidnapped at a beach resort by six suspected Moslem guerrillas on Sunday.
"Very, very good experience," Takayama told reporters.
He showed bruises on his legs suffered while struggling up the mountain at the orders of his captors.
The military said it believed the kidnappers belonged to the fundamentalist Abu Sayyaf Moslem guerrillas who are fighting for an Islamic state on the southern island of Mindanao and nearby islands.

"I have to go back first to Tokyo and then I will think again if I will be back (in the Philippines)," Takayama said, when asked about his plans. Two of the kidnappers were shot and killed by government forces before Takayama and his companions were rescued, Sarangani governor Priscilla Chiongbian told Reuters.
Police earlier said another kidnapper was killed in a shootout on Sunday a few hours after six heavily armed men kidnapped Takayama and his companions.
Another Filipino on the beach was killed by the kidnappers before they took Takayama and the others away, police said.
"The police are still chasing the rest of the kidnappers up to now," she said by telephone.
Takayama has been a resident of nearby General Santos city for the past few years, running a company that exports mangoes and other food to Japan.
In Manila, officials of the watchdog Citizens Action Against Crime (CAAC) said the latest of a series of kidnappings could hurt business confidence in the country.
Japan is the Philippines' third largest foreign investor and largest aid donor.
Kidnap-for-ransom has become a booming trade in a country Fortune Magazine has dubbed "Asia's kidnap capital". Police said the label was unfair.
The southern Philippines, home to bandits and Moslem separatist rebels, is especially notorious.

At least 89 people were kidnapped around the country in the first four months of this year with gangs collecting 152 million pesos ($5.7 million) in ransom from victims' relatives, statistics compiled by citizens' groups showed.
The amount more than doubled that collected by kidnappers for all of last year when they got at least 69 million pesos in ransom from families of 241 kidnap victims.
In 1995, kidnap gangs seized 199 people and collected at least 112 million pesos in ransom, the citizens' groups said.

Takayama was the first Japanese abducted in the country since two Filipino soldiers kidnapped a construction firm owner in Manila in January 1994. He was freed after payment of seven million pesos in ransom.
Another Japanese, Nobuyki Wakaoji, then a director at Mitsui and Co Ltd, was the victim in one of the country's biggest kidnapping cases.
Abducted in 1986, Wakaoji was released months later after payment of a $3 million ransom. Two Filipino masterminds of the kidnapping were sentenced to life imprisonment in 1992.
Widespread belief that soldiers and police protect kidnappers has discouraged Filipinos from reporting to the authorities.
Kidnapping incidents have continued despite President Fidel Ramos's order to the military last month to take over the job of hunting down the gangs, saying the army had more firepower to fight them.
